entries.meaning: Bharata bathed in Prayāga, bowed his head to the sage with the whole company, and respectfully took the sage’s command and blessing. After repeated prostration and humble words, he gathered guides who knew the road and every capable companion, then set out toward Citrakūṭa with his mind fixed there. He placed a hand upon Guha’s arm and walked like love itself in bodily form. He had no footwear or shade above his head; guileless love, discipline, vow, and duty were his protection. In gentle speech he asked his friend to recount the road taken by Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa. Whenever he saw a tree or place where Rāma had stayed, the love in his heart could not be restrained. The gods, seeing his state, rained flowers; earth and road became soft and auspicious. Clouds offered shade, pleasant winds blew, and water appeared—but the road was never made so kind for Rāma as it became for Bharata.

Countless moving and unmoving creatures along the road had once caught the Lord’s glance or looked upon him; all became fit for the highest state, and Bharata’s sight now cured their worldly sickness. This was not a great matter for Bharata, within whose mind Rāma always dwelt: even those who utter ‘Rāma’ once become people able to cross and carry others across the world. Bharata was Rāma’s beloved younger brother, so how could the road not become a giver of blessing? Perfected beings, saints, and eminent sages said this and rejoiced when they saw him. Indra, however, became anxious at Bharata’s influence; the good world is good to the good but perverse to the perverse. He asked his guru to contrive that Rāma and Bharata not meet. Rāma is restrained by love and Bharata a loving ocean, Indra argued; the settled affair seemed about to unravel, so some tested deception should be attempted.

Hearing Indra’s words, Bṛhaspati smiled: the thousand-eyed god, he thought, was acting blind. He warned: ‘If anyone uses illusion against the servant of the Lord of illusion, it recoils upon the schemer, king of gods. Earlier you acted after reading Rāma’s intention; an evil device now would bring harm. Know Raghunātha’s nature: he is not angry at anyone for an offense against himself, but whoever harms his devotee burns in the fire of Rāma’s wrath. This history is famous in the world and Vedas; Durvāsas knows that majesty. Who loves Rāma like Bharata? The world repeats Rāma’s name, while Rāma repeats his. Never even bring harm to Raghubara’s devotee into your mind, lord of immortals; it brings dishonor here and hereafter, sorrow every day, and an accumulation of grief.’

Bṛhaspati continued: ‘Hear my counsel, Indra: a servant is supremely dear to Rāma. He takes pleasure in the servant’s service and treats the servant’s enemy as an even greater enemy. Although he is equal toward all, without attachment or anger, and accepts neither sin nor merit, virtue nor fault, he established a world governed by action, in which each tastes the fruit of what one does. Yet his apparently equal or unequal dealings accord with the hearts of devotee and nondevotee. Attribute-free, untouched, free of pride, and of one essence, Rāma becomes manifest with attributes under the power of a devotee’s love. He always preserves his servant’s preference; the Vedas, Purāṇas, saints, and gods attest it. Knowing this, abandon crookedness and cherish lovely love for Bharata’s feet. Rāma’s devotees are devoted to others’ welfare, grieve at others’ pain, and are compassionate; do not fear Bharata, the crest-jewel among devotees.’

‘The Lord is true to his word and works for the gods’ welfare, while Bharata follows Rāma’s command. Your own interest has made you agitated; the fault lies not in Bharata but in your delusion.’ Hearing his guru’s excellent words, Indra rejoiced and his shame vanished. Gladly showering flowers, he began praising Bharata’s disposition. As Bharata continued along the road, sages and perfected beings marveled at his condition. Whenever he breathed the name ‘Rāma’ with a sigh, love seemed to surge around him on every side. His words melted even thunderbolts and stones; the citizens’ love cannot be described. Camping midway, the company reached the Yamunā; seeing its dark water, their eyes filled with tears. Gazing upon the excellent water in Raghubara’s complexion, the company nearly sank in the ocean of separation, but mounted the ship of discernment.

They camped that day on the Yamunā’s bank, and in due time every convenience became available to all. During the night innumerable boats arrived from every landing place. At dawn everyone crossed in a single round of ferrying and rewarded Guha for his service. After bathing and bowing to the river they continued, with the Niṣāda king and the two brothers. Eminent sages and their vehicles went ahead, the royal company followed behind, and behind them walked the simply dressed brothers, without ornaments and on foot. Servants, friends, and ministers’ sons accompanied them as they remembered Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, and Raghunātha. Wherever Rāma had lodged or rested, they made loving prostrations. Roadside men and women heard of the company, abandoned home and work, and ran out; seeing Bharata’s form and love, they rejoiced and gained the fruit of birth.

The village women lovingly asked one another: ‘Friend, can these be Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa?’ Their age, body, complexion, beauty, character, affection, and gait were just alike. ‘But the dress is different, friend, Sītā is not with them, and a fourfold army moves in front. Their faces are not cheerful and their hearts seem afflicted—these differences create doubt.’ The women accepted one woman’s reasoning, called none wiser than she, and praised her fulfilled words. Another then sweetly told with love the whole course of events by which Rāma’s royal happiness was broken, and the women again praised fortunate Bharata’s character, affection, and nature. ‘He travels on foot, eating fruit, having abandoned the kingdom his father gave, and goes to win over Raghubara—who today can equal Bharata?’

The story of Bharata’s brotherly devotion and conduct removes the sorrow and faults of those who tell and hear it. The women said: ‘Whatever little we can say is true, friend—why would Rāma’s brother not be like Rāma? We women have seen Bharata with his younger brother and count ourselves blessed. Hearing his virtues and seeing his state, we regret that Kaikeyī was not a mother worthy of such a son.’ Another said the queen was not to blame; destiny had done it all and merely appeared favorable to them. ‘What are we—small women of low family, lacking worldly, Vedic, and ritual standing—who live in a bad region, poor villages, and humble homes; and what is this vision, the ripened fruit of merit?’ Such joy and wonder came to every village, as though a wish-fulfilling tree had grown in a desert. At Bharata’s sight the road opened the people’s fortune, as though residents of Siṃhala suddenly found Prayāga near at hand.

As Bharata went, he heard accounts of Rāma’s virtues joined with praise of his own, and remembered Raghunātha. Seeing holy places, hermitages, and divine dwellings, the travelers bowed and immersed themselves in their waters. Inwardly they asked one boon: love for the lotus feet of Sītā and Rāma. They met Kirātas, Kols, forest dwellers, Vaikhānasa hermits, religious students, ascetics, and renunciants; bowing, they asked each one where in the forest Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, and Vaidehī were. These people told all the Lord’s news and, seeing Bharata, gained the fruit of life. Anyone who said, ‘We saw them well,’ became as dear as Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa themselves. Thus they asked everyone courteously and listened to the story of Rāma’s forest exile. They camped that day and departed at dawn remembering Raghunātha, the whole company sharing Bharata’s longing for Rāma’s sight.

Auspicious signs appeared for everyone: eyes and arms throbbed favorably. Bharata and the company grew eager—Rāma would be met and burning sorrow extinguished. Each formed hopes according to the heart while traveling, all saturated with the nectar of affection. Their limbs slackened, feet wavered on the path, and they spoke helplessly under love’s power. At that moment Guha showed them the naturally beautiful crown among mountains, near whose riverbank the two heroes lived with Sītā. On seeing it all prostrated and cried, ‘Victory to Rāma, life of Jānakī!’ The royal company was so immersed in love that it seemed Raghurāja was returning to Ayodhyā. Bharata’s love then cannot be told even by Śeṣa; for a poet it is as inaccessible as the bliss of Brahman is to one born in the soiled sense of ‘I’ and ‘mine.’
